title: A thing, the thing, or some: articles and gender
summary: Choose articles for identified things, general categories and uncounted quantities; combine them with à and de.
objectives: Distinguish definite, indefinite and partitive articles.
Use reliable gender clues without treating them as guarantees.
Form au, aux, du and des and recognise familiar definite-article contexts.

sections.title: Choose the noun's gender, then decide whether it is identified
paragraphs: Indefinite articles introduce a countable item: un (masculine), une (feminine), des (plural). Definite articles identify something known or a whole category: le, la, les. Le and la become l' before a vowel or silent h; plural les does not elide. Un hôtel (m., a hotel) therefore gives l'hôtel. With an aspirated h, a conventional sound boundary blocks elision even though h is not pronounced: le héros (the hero). Learn such nouns with their article.

Endings are clues, not proof. -tion and -sion are usually feminine, as in une invitation and une décision; -ment and -age are often masculine, as in un document and un garage. But une page, une image and une plage (a beach) are feminine, while un million is masculine despite -ion. A final written e alone does not establish gender: un problème is masculine.
points: A new singular countable noun normally needs an article or another determiner.
A noun's grammatical gender remains the same when its article becomes l'.

examples.english: I have an invitation. The invitation is here.
examples.note: Introduce the item, then refer to the identified item.
Un problème is masculine despite its final e.
Une page is an exception to the common masculine -age pattern.

mistakes.why: Hôtel has a silent h and requires elision; it is also masculine.

sections.title: A portion uses a partitive; a general preference uses the definite article
paragraphs: For an unspecified amount, use du before a masculine noun, de la before a feminine noun, de l' before a vowel or silent h, and des for plural quantities. These are called partitive articles when they present an uncounted portion; des also serves as the plural indefinite article with countable items. English often leaves some or any unspoken; French normally keeps the article.

A whole category takes le, la or les, especially after verbs expressing likes: aimer le thé means to like tea generally. Contrast drinking some tea with liking tea as a category. Un thé can instead mean one serving of tea.
points: Du pain is some bread; le pain can mean the identified bread or bread in general.
Vocabulary: le pain (m., bread), la soupe (f., soup), l'eau (f., water), les épinards (m. plural, spinach).

examples.french: Je prends **du** pain et **de la** soupe.
examples.english: I am having some bread and soup.
We have some water and spinach.
examples.note: Elision before eau; plural des with épinards.

examples.french: J'aime **le** thé, mais je prends **un** café.
examples.english: I like tea, but I am having a coffee.
examples.note: The general category contrasts with one serving.

mistakes.why: De la elides to de l' before eau.

sections.title: À and de combine with le and les
paragraphs: When the preposition à meets definite le, write au; à + les gives aux. De + le gives du; de + les gives des. There is no contraction with la or l': à la, à l', de la, de l'. A preposition is a linking word such as to, at or from. Du can therefore be either a quantity article or the combination de + le; read the sentence to decide.
points: À + le = au; à + les = aux; de + le = du; de + les = des.

examples.french: Elle va **au** marché, puis **à la** banque.
examples.english: She goes to the market, then to the bank.
examples.note: Le marché (m., market) contracts; la banque (f., bank) does not.
Here du means de + le, not some.

examples.english: He speaks to the neighbours' children.
examples.note: Aux combines à + les; des combines de + les.

mistakes.why: À + le must contract when le is the article.

sections.title: French keeps the definite article in several places English omits it
paragraphs: Use definite articles for languages as nouns and academic subjects: le français, les mathématiques. But after parler a language is commonly bare: parler français. Titles normally take the article when speaking about someone: le professeur Martin, la docteure Roy. Direct address usually omits it: Bonjour, docteure !

For body parts whose owner is clear, French often prefers the definite article, especially with a reflexive verb: elle se lave les mains. Possessives remain possible when ownership or contrast needs emphasis. Familiar clothing expressions also use the definite article, such as enlever le manteau, especially when a reflexive form identifies the wearer. This is not a ban on mon manteau (my coat).
points: Vocabulary: une main (f., hand), un manteau (m., coat), le français (m., French language).

examples.french: **Le** français est utile. Je parle français.
examples.english: French is useful. I speak French.
examples.note: Language as subject has an article; after parler it is omitted here.
Mentioning a professional by title differs from addressing her.
The reflexive construction makes the owner clear.
The reflexive form identifies whose coat is being removed.

practice.explanation: Décision is feminine; -sion is a useful clue.

practice.prompt: Use a partitive article: 'Je mange ___ soupe.' (soupe is feminine).
practice.explanation: An unspecified amount of feminine soupe takes de la.

practice.prompt: Combine à + les into one word.
practice.explanation: The contraction is compulsory with the article les.

practice.prompt: For a general preference, complete 'J'aime ___ pain.'
practice.explanation: A general category takes the definite article.

practice.prompt: Supply the partitive for an unspecified amount: 'Il boit ___ lait.' (lait is masculine).
practice.explanation: Du introduces an unspecified amount of masculine lait.

practice.prompt: Use a partitive article: 'Nous avons ___ huile.' (huile is feminine with silent h).
Supply de + le: 'C'est la clé ___ bureau.'
practice.explanation: De + le bureau becomes du bureau.

practice.prompt: Supply à plus the definite article: 'Je vais ___ école.' (école is feminine).
practice.explanation: Before école use l'; à l' does not contract.

practice.prompt: Choose the indefinite article for one item: '___ image'.
practice.explanation: Image is a feminine exception to the common -age pattern.

practice.prompt: Supply the usual definite article: 'Elle se brosse ___ dents.'
practice.explanation: The reflexive construction identifies whose teeth; dents is plural.

practice.prompt: Supply the definite article: '___ mathématiques sont utiles.'
practice.explanation: An academic subject used as a noun takes the article.

practice.prompt: You are talking about, not addressing, Professor Laurent. Choose the normal wording.
practice.explanation: Use the article when referring to someone by this title.

practice.prompt: Use the article for an unspecified plural quantity: 'Je prends ___ épinards.'
practice.explanation: Épinards is plural; an unspecified quantity takes des.

practice.prompt: Combine de + les in 'les noms ___ élèves'.
Supply le or les in the usual clothing expression: 'Il s'enlève ___ chapeau.'
practice.explanation: One masculine chapeau takes le; the wearer is identified by s'.

practice.prompt: Does every noun ending in -e have feminine gender?
practice.explanation: Un problème is masculine; learn each noun with its article.

production_task.prompt: Describe a simple lunch: say what you have in unspecified quantities, then name one food you like in general. Use three different article forms.
production_task.model_answer: J'ai du pain, de la soupe et de l'eau. J'aime les légumes.
production_task.translation: I have some bread, soup and water. I like vegetables.
rubric: Use a definite article for a general preference.
Match gender and number and elide before a vowel.
